DNA sequencing. It's the process of determining the precise order of nucleotide bases—A, T, G, and C—along a DNA molecule. Modern sequencing underpins genomics, diagnostics, and evolutionary studies, with methods ranging from Sanger sequencing for single molecules as the gold standard to next-generation sequencing that can process millions of reads in parallel. Sanger sequencing, the original method from 1977, uses chain-terminating nucleotides called ddNTPs to halt DNA synthesis at each base. This generates a ladder of fragments differing by one base that are separated by gel or capillary electrophoresis. Next-generation sequencing is massively parallel. DNA is fragmented, amplified on a chip or bead, and millions of reads are generated simultaneously, enabling whole-genome sequencing at much lower cost per base. Read length matters significantly. Sanger yields long, accurate reads around one thousand base pairs, while NGS offers short reads of one hundred to three hundred base pairs or long reads of ten thousand or more base pairs in newer technologies, each suited to different applications. Short reads from NGS must be computationally stitched together to reconstruct the original genome in a process called de novo assembly, though existing reference genomes speed this step considerably. Sanger sequencing has roughly one error per ten thousand bases, while NGS error rates vary by platform but are offset by coverage depth—reading the same region multiple times. Sequencing is now common for variant discovery, pathogen identification, cancer genomics, and microbiome studies. This technique connects naturally to DNA as the molecule being sequenced, PCR which typically amplifies templates before sequencing, gel electrophoresis as the classical method for resolving Sanger sequencing fragments, DNA polymerase as the enzyme that extends the DNA strand during sequencing reactions, and the human genome project as the landmark effort that drove sequencing technology innovation.
